prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: 주요 아파트 실거래가 추이(2023–2024) (language ko).
Grid: 6 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "단지명" spans 1 col × 2 row; "전용면적" spans 1 col × 2 row; "2023년" spans 2 col × 1 row; "2024년" spans 2 col × 1 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "단지명" · longest unbreakable word 13px · one-line width 105px
  col 2: header "전용면적" · longest unbreakable word 45px · one-line width 60px
  col 3: header "2023년 › 최저" · longest unbreakable word 41px · one-line width 75px
  col 4: header "2023년 › 최고" · longest unbreakable word 41px · one-line width 76px
  col 5: header "2024년 › 최저" · longest unbreakable word 41px · one-line width 75px
  col 6: header "2024년 › 최고" · longest unbreakable word 41px · one-line width 76px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"poor","why":"The four price columns are consistent and most amounts break at a useful point, but apartment names wrap heavily and the last area value splits within its number."},"B":{"grade":"poor","why":"Price columns remain easy to compare, but narrow row headers fragment apartment names more than in A, and the last area value splits within its number."},"C":{"grade":"bad","why":"Apartment names run almost one character per line, making row identification difficult and leaving large vertical gaps across the price columns."},"D":{"grade":"bad","why":"Area numbers stay intact, but the extremely narrow first column turns apartment names into long vertical strings and makes the table difficult to scan."},"E":{"grade":"bad","why":"Area values and many prices split within their numbers, making figures difficult to read and compare; apartment names also wrap heavily."}},"best":["A"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"A and B are very close; the distinction rests mainly on the wrapping of the final apartment name."}
